topics.title: Force, Aristotle's fallacy and Galileo's inclines

learn.hook: Stop pedalling your cycle and it slows down. For 2000 years people concluded that motion needs a constant push. They were wrong.
points: Kinematics describes motion; dynamics asks what causes motion and changes in motion. The answer is force.
A force is needed to change a body's velocity (speed or direction), not to keep it moving. Forces may act by contact (push, friction, tension) or at a distance (gravity, magnetic, electric).
Aristotle's fallacy: an external force is needed to keep a body moving uniformly. Wrong, because he missed friction and air resistance, which oppose motion; the push only cancels them.
Galileo's inclined planes: a ball speeds up rolling down, slows down rolling up, and on a horizontal plane its speed should stay constant if there is no friction.

example.q: A cart is pushed along a road at constant speed with a 50 N force. Why does it need the push at all, and what does that say about Aristotle's idea?
steps: At constant velocity, the net force on the cart is zero.
So the 50 N push must be balanced by 50 N of friction and air resistance.
The push cancels opposing forces; it is not needed for motion itself. Aristotle's view overlooked friction.
example.answer: The push only balances friction; net force is zero

learn.reallife: A hockey puck on smooth ice at an indoor rink in Gurugram glides far without any push because friction is tiny.

teach.ask: Gappu says, 'My toy car stops when I stop pushing, so things need a push to keep moving.' Explain why he's wrong using Aristotle and Galileo.
teach.praise: Friction was the sneaky villain! Without it, my car would roll on forever.
teach.nudge: What force did Aristotle forget? And what is force really needed for?

learn.hook: Pull a tablecloth fast enough and the dishes stay put. That stubbornness of matter has a name: inertia.
points: Galileo's double incline: a ball rolling down one incline climbs the other to nearly the same height. Make the second incline gentler and it travels farther; make it horizontal and, without friction, it would roll forever.
So rest and uniform straight-line motion are equivalent states: in both, no net force acts.
Inertia is the resistance of a body to any change in its state of rest or uniform motion. Mass is the measure of inertia.

Ancient Indian thought: the Vaisheshika idea of 'vega' (a tendency to keep moving in a straight line) came close to inertia, and Bhaskara II's (1150 CE) 'tatkaliki gati' anticipated instantaneous motion.
Newton's first law: every body continues in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless compelled by an external net force to change that state.

example.q: In Galileo's double incline, the first plane is released from 20 cm height. The second plane is made less steep. What happens?
steps: Without friction, the ball rises to the same 20 cm height.
A gentler slope means a longer path to reach 20 cm.
With the slope reduced to zero, it never reaches 20 cm, so it rolls on forever.
example.answer: It travels farther; on a level plane it would never stop

learn.reallife: When a spent stage of an ISRO rocket separates in space, it keeps coasting at the velocity it had: inertia at work.

teach.ask: Gappu asks why passengers' heads jerk and why a tablecloth trick works. Explain inertia and state Newton's first law.
teach.praise: Matter is lazy about changing what it's doing: that's inertia. And only a net force can change it!
teach.nudge: What property keeps things doing what they were doing? What does it take to change that?

topics.title: First law in action, and momentum

learn.hook: A cricket ball and a tennis ball at the same speed: one you can catch bare-handed, the other stings. The difference is momentum.
points: First law, equivalent form: if the net external force on a body is zero, its acceleration is zero (and vice versa).
A book on a table: weight down is balanced by the normal force up, so a = 0. A spaceship far from all stars needs no engine to keep moving uniformly.
Passengers lurch backward when a bus starts suddenly and forward when it brakes: their bodies tend to keep their earlier state.
An astronaut who leaves an accelerating spaceship has zero acceleration the moment he is outside (no force from the ship, gravity negligible in deep space).
Momentum p = mv is a vector along v. Catching a fast ball, stopping a bullet, or a karate chop all show that the effect of a blow depends on momentum and on how fast it changes.

example.q: A spaceship in deep space accelerates at 100 m s⁻². An astronaut drifts out of the hatch. What is his acceleration just after leaving?
steps: Inside, the ship's floor pushes him, giving 100 m s⁻².
Outside, nothing pushes him and gravity from distant stars is negligible.
Net force = 0, so his acceleration is 0 (he keeps the velocity he had).

learn.reallife: In a crowded DTC bus, standing passengers grab the handle when it suddenly brakes, because their bodies keep moving forward by inertia.

teach.ask: Gappu fell forward when the bird-bus braked and blamed the driver for pushing him. Explain what really happened, and what momentum is.
teach.praise: Nobody pushed me; my body just kept going! And heavier, faster things carry more momentum.
teach.nudge: Did a force push you forward, or did your body just keep doing something? What is momentum?

topics.title: Newton's second law: F = dp/dt and F = ma

learn.hook: Push a shopping trolley at a supermarket: empty, it zips; loaded, it crawls. Same push, different acceleration.
points: Second law: the rate of change of momentum of a body equals the net applied force and takes place in the direction of the force: F = dp/dt.
For constant mass, F = m dv/dt = ma. 1 newton = force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m s⁻²: 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻².
F = 0 gives a = 0, so the second law agrees with the first.
Component form: Fₓ = maₓ, F_y = ma_y, F_z = ma_z. A force changes only the velocity component along it (a force ⊥ v changes direction, not speed).
The law is local: the acceleration at an instant depends on the net force at that same instant, not on past forces.

example.q: A net force of 20 N acts on a 4 kg block. Find the acceleration and the velocity after 3 s, starting from rest.

learn.reallife: When a cricket ball leaves the bowler's hand, its acceleration depends only on the forces at that instant (gravity and air), not on the bowler's push a moment ago.

topics.title: Second law in action: bullets, impulse and batsmen

learn.hook: A batsman meets a 140 km/h bouncer for a few milliseconds. In that blink, the force on the bat can reach thousands of newtons.
points: The second law applies to a particle, and also to a rigid body or a whole system, using the net EXTERNAL force and the acceleration of the system.
Impulse = F × Δt = change in momentum Δp. Impulsive forces are large and act for a very short time (bat on ball, hammer on nail); we measure their effect by Δp.
Bullet stopped in a block: find a from v² = u² + 2as, then F = ma.
If y = ut + ½gt² describes a particle (x-motion uniform), then a = g along y, so F = mg along y: a constant force gives a parabolic path.
Ball hit straight back at the same speed: Δp = m(v − (−v)) = 2mv.

example.q: A 0.15 kg cricket ball moving at 20 m s⁻¹ is hit straight back at 20 m s⁻¹. Find the impulse and the average force if contact lasts 0.01 s.
steps: Take the ball's return direction as +: initial p = −0.15 × 20 = −3 kg m s⁻¹, final p = +3 kg m s⁻¹.
Impulse = Δp = 3 − (−3) = 6 N s.
Average force = 6/0.01 = 600 N.

learn.reallife: Fielders pull their hands back while catching to increase the contact time, reducing the force for the same change in momentum.

teach.ask: Gappu caught a falling acorn with stiff wings and it hurt! Explain impulse and why moving the wings back helps.
teach.praise: Same momentum change, more time, less force. I'll catch the next acorn softly!
teach.nudge: What does impulse equal? If the time is longer, what happens to the force?

learn.hook: When you push a wall, the wall pushes you back just as hard. Then why don't the two pushes cancel? This is the most misunderstood law in physics.
points: Third law: to every action there is always an equal and opposite reaction. F_AB = −F_BA (force on A by B equals minus force on B by A).
Action and reaction act at the same instant on DIFFERENT bodies, so they never cancel each other.
There is no cause and effect between them: either force can be called the action.
In a system of bodies, internal forces come in third-law pairs and cancel; so only external forces affect the motion of the whole system.
Two colliding billiard balls exert equal and opposite forces for the same time, so they receive equal and opposite impulses.

example.q: A 50 kg girl on skates pushes a 25 kg boy on skates with 100 N. Find each one's acceleration.
steps: The boy gets 100 N forward: a = 100/25 = 4 m s⁻².
By the third law, the girl gets 100 N backward: a = 100/50 = 2 m s⁻² backward.
Equal forces, unequal accelerations, because masses differ.
example.answer: Boy 4 m s⁻², girl 2 m s⁻² opposite

learn.reallife: When an Indian Navy sailor fires a deck gun, the gun recoils: the shell pushes back on the gun with the same force the gun pushes the shell.

teach.ask: Gappu says, 'If action and reaction are equal and opposite, they cancel, so nothing can ever move!' Explain where his reasoning breaks.
teach.praise: They act on DIFFERENT bodies, so they can't cancel each other. Phew, I can still fly!
teach.nudge: Do action and reaction act on the same body or on different bodies?

topics.title: Rockets, recoil and conservation of momentum

learn.hook: Chandrayaan-3's rocket had nothing to 'push against' in space. It moved by throwing gas backward: momentum must be conserved.
points: Third-law examples: walking (foot pushes ground back, ground pushes you forward), rowing (oar pushes water back), rocket (rocket pushes gas backward, gas pushes rocket forward), gun recoil.
Law of conservation of momentum: the total momentum of an isolated system (no net external force) stays constant.
Derivation for a collision: F_AB Δt = Δp_A and F_BA Δt = Δp_B; since F_AB = −F_BA, Δp_A + Δp_B = 0.
Recoil of a gun (initially at rest): 0 = m_b v_b + M V → V = −m_b v_b/M.
A shell exploding in flight: internal forces cannot change the total momentum; the fragments' momenta add up to the shell's momentum just before the explosion.

example.q: A 4 kg gun fires a 0.02 kg bullet at 400 m s⁻¹. Find the recoil velocity of the gun.
steps: Initial momentum = 0.
V = −8/4 = −2 m s⁻¹ (opposite to the bullet).

learn.reallife: ISRO's PSLV and GSLV rockets throw out exhaust gases at kilometres per second; the forward momentum of the rocket equals the backward momentum of the gas.

games.title: Deriving conservation of momentum in a collision
items: Force on A by B acts for time Δt: F_AB Δt = Δp_A
Force on B by A acts for the same Δt: F_BA Δt = Δp_B
Third law: F_AB = −F_BA
So Δp_A = −Δp_B
Hence p_A + p_B is unchanged

quiz.q: A 3 kg shell at rest explodes into two pieces. A 1 kg piece flies off at 40 m s⁻¹. The speed of the other piece in m s⁻¹ is
quiz.explain: 0 = 1 × 40 + 2 × v → v = −20 m s⁻¹, so its speed is 20 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction.
quiz.mistake: Uses the total mass 3 kg for the second piece

quiz.q: Momentum of a system is conserved when
options: The net external force on it is zero
quiz.explain: Internal forces cancel in pairs; only external forces can change total momentum.
quiz.mistake: Thinks internal forces must vanish

quiz.q: A rocket moves forward in empty space because
options: It pushes exhaust gas backward and the gas pushes it forward
quiz.explain: Third law and momentum conservation: no air is needed.
quiz.mistake: Thinks rockets need air to push against

quiz.q: A shell moving horizontally at 10 m s⁻¹ explodes into two equal halves. One half falls straight down with zero horizontal speed just after the explosion. The other half's horizontal speed in m s⁻¹ is
quiz.explain: Horizontal momentum: m × 10 = (m/2)(0) + (m/2)v → v = 20 m s⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Thinks each half keeps 10 m s⁻¹

quiz.q: When we walk, the force that pushes us forward is
options: Our muscles pushing on our own body
The ground's frictional push on our feet
quiz.explain: Our feet push the ground backward; the ground's reaction (static friction) pushes us forward.
quiz.mistake: Thinks internal muscle forces alone move the body

quiz.q: Two skaters at rest push each other apart. Skater A (40 kg) moves at 3 m s⁻¹. Skater B (60 kg) moves at (in m s⁻¹)
quiz.explain: 40 × 3 = 60 × v → v = 2 m s⁻¹, opposite to A.
quiz.mistake: Assumes equal speeds

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The total momentum of a shell is unchanged just after it explodes in flight.
Reason (R): The forces of the explosion are internal to the shell–fragments system.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Internal forces cancel in pairs and gravity acts only negligibly during the brief explosion, so total momentum is conserved. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks an explosion creates momentum

teach.ask: Gappu thinks rockets fly by pushing against air, so they shouldn't work in space. Explain using the third law and conservation of momentum.
teach.praise: The rocket throws gas back and the gas shoves the rocket forward. No air needed!
teach.nudge: What does the rocket push on? What stays the same for the rocket plus its gas?

learn.hook: A street lamp hangs perfectly still from two wires. The wires' pulls and the lamp's weight form a perfect closed triangle.
points: A particle is in equilibrium when the net external force on it is zero (it is at rest or moving uniformly).
Two forces in equilibrium must be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction along the same line.
Three concurrent forces in equilibrium can be drawn head to tail as a closed triangle (triangle law of forces); many forces form a closed polygon.
Component conditions: ΣFₓ = 0, ΣF_y = 0, ΣF_z = 0.
Method: draw the forces on the point (e.g. the knot), resolve them along x and y, and solve ΣFₓ = 0 and ΣF_y = 0.

example.q: A 4 kg mass hangs from a string. A horizontal force F pulls the mass aside until the string makes θ with the vertical, where tan θ = 0.75. Find F and the tension (g = 10 m s⁻²).
steps: Vertical: T cos θ = mg = 40 N.
Horizontal: T sin θ = F.

learn.reallife: Engineers designing the overhead electric lines for Indian Railways' electrified tracks balance the tensions and weights at every support point.

games.title: Solving an equilibrium problem
items: Choose the point or body in equilibrium
Draw all forces acting on it
Choose x and y axes
Resolve each force into components
Set ΣFₓ = 0 and ΣF_y = 0 and solve

games.title: Equilibrium facts
items: A body moving with constant velocity is in equilibrium.
Net force is zero.
Two forces of 5 N and 7 N can keep a particle in equilibrium.
Two forces must be equal and opposite.
Three forces in equilibrium form a closed triangle when drawn head to tail.
Their resultant is zero.
A body at the top of its vertical throw is in equilibrium.
Gravity acts; net force is not zero.
Forces of 3 N, 4 N and 5 N can be in equilibrium.
They can form a closed 3-4-5 triangle.

quiz.q: Which set of three forces CANNOT keep a particle in equilibrium?
quiz.explain: Three forces can balance only if each is ≤ the sum of the other two. 7 > 2 + 3, so no closed triangle.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any three forces can be arranged to balance

quiz.q: A 10 kg mass hangs at rest from a rope (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). The tension in the rope in N is
quiz.explain: Equilibrium: T = mg = 10 × 9.8 = 98 N.
quiz.mistake: Gives the mass instead of the weight

quiz.q: A 20 kg mass hangs from two strings, each making 60° with the vertical (g = 10 m s⁻², cos 60° = 0.5). The tension in each string in N is
quiz.mistake: Assumes each string carries half the weight

quiz.q: A 6 kg mass hangs from a string and is pulled aside by a horizontal force till the string makes 45° with the vertical (g = 10 m s⁻²). The horizontal force in N is
quiz.explain: tan 45° = F/mg → F = mg = 60 N.
quiz.mistake: Uses sin 45° instead of tan 45°

quiz.q: The conditions for equilibrium of a particle in component form are
quiz.explain: Every component of the net force must vanish.
quiz.mistake: Checks only the vertical direction

quiz.q: Two forces acting on a particle keep it in equilibrium. They must be
options: Of any magnitude if they are opposite
Equal in magnitude, opposite in direction and along the same line
quiz.explain: Only then is their sum zero.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that magnitudes must match

quiz.q: Forces of 3 N east and 4 N north act on a particle. The third force needed for equilibrium has magnitude (in N)
quiz.explain: It must cancel the resultant √(9 + 16) = 5 N, pointing south-west.
quiz.mistake: Adds the magnitudes

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A lamp hanging from two wires is in equilibrium.
Reason (R): The vector sum of the two tensions and the weight is zero.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Zero net force is the meaning of equilibrium, and R gives it. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks equilibrium needs no forces at all

teach.ask: Gappu is hanging from two twigs and wonders why he doesn't fall. Explain the conditions for equilibrium and how to find the tension in each twig.
teach.praise: My weight is balanced by the two pulls; the forces make a closed triangle. Safe and sound!
teach.nudge: What must the total force be? How do you find each tension using components?

topics.title: Common forces: gravity, normal, tension and spring

learn.hook: When you sit on a chair, the chair pushes up on you with exactly your weight. Where does that push come from? From electric forces between atoms!
points: Gravity acts at a distance; most other mechanical forces (normal, friction, tension, spring) are contact forces.
Normal reaction N is the component of contact force perpendicular to the surfaces in contact.
Tension acts along a string, pulling on the bodies attached; for a massless string it is the same throughout.
Spring force F = −kx: a restoring force proportional to extension or compression x, directed opposite to it (k is the spring constant).
Contact forces ultimately come from electrical forces between the charged particles (electrons and nuclei) of the surfaces.

example.q: A spring of spring constant 200 N m⁻¹ is stretched by 5 cm. Find the restoring force.
steps: Magnitude 10 N, directed back towards the natural length.

learn.reallife: The shock absorbers of a motorbike and the spring balance at a sabzi mandi both rely on F = −kx.

games.title: Force ↔ description
pairs: Perpendicular to the surface of contact
Pull along a string or rope
Parallel to the surface of contact

quiz.q: A spring with k = 400 N m⁻¹ is compressed by 0.05 m. The magnitude of the spring force in N is
quiz.mistake: Divides instead of multiplying

quiz.q: The negative sign in F = −kx shows that the spring force
options: Is opposite to the displacement from natural length
quiz.explain: It is a restoring force, always pointing back towards the natural length.
quiz.mistake: Reads the minus sign as a negative magnitude

quiz.q: A 5 kg block rests on a horizontal table (g = 10 m s⁻²). The normal force on it in N is
quiz.explain: Vertical equilibrium: N = mg = 50 N.
quiz.mistake: Gives the mass instead of the weight

quiz.q: Contact forces like normal force and friction ultimately arise from
options: Electrical forces between charged constituents of matter
quiz.explain: Electrons and nuclei of the two surfaces interact electrically.
quiz.mistake: Thinks gravity between atoms is responsible

quiz.q: In a massless string passing over a frictionless pulley, the tension is
quiz.explain: A massless string needs no net force, so the tension is uniform.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the pulley changes the tension

quiz.q: The normal force on a block on a surface is
options: Perpendicular to the surface of contact
quiz.explain: It is perpendicular to the surface; on an incline N = mg cos θ, not mg.
quiz.mistake: Thinks N is always equal to mg

quiz.q: A 2 kg block hangs from a spring of k = 196 N m⁻¹ and is at rest (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). The extension in m is
quiz.mistake: Divides k by weight

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Friction and normal reaction are both components of the contact force between two surfaces.
Reason (R): Friction always acts in the direction of motion of a body.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true. R is false: friction opposes relative motion (or impending motion) between the surfaces.
quiz.mistake: Thinks friction pushes bodies along

teach.ask: Gappu thinks the chair 'just sits there' and does nothing while he sits on it. Explain normal force, tension, spring force, and where contact forces come from.
teach.praise: The chair pushes me up with electric forces between atoms! And springs push back with kx.
teach.nudge: Which way does the chair push you, and why? What kind of force is behind all contact forces?

learn.hook: Push a heavy almirah: nothing happens, then suddenly it jerks into motion. Static friction just gave up its maximum value.
points: Static friction f_s opposes impending relative motion. It is self-adjusting: it equals the applied force up to a limit f_s(max) = μ_s N.
Laws of friction: limiting friction is independent of the area of contact and proportional to the normal reaction N.
Kinetic friction f_k = μ_k N acts once sliding begins, opposing relative motion. μ_k < μ_s, and f_k is roughly independent of speed.
Angle of repose: a block on an incline is just about to slide when tan θ = μ_s.
Rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction; that's why wheels and ball bearings are used.

example.q: A 10 kg box rests on a floor with μ_s = 0.5 and μ_k = 0.4 (g = 10 m s⁻²). What friction acts if you push with (a) 30 N, (b) 60 N?
steps: (a) 30 N < 50 N: box stays; static friction = 30 N.
(b) 60 N > 50 N: box slides; kinetic friction = 0.4 × 100 = 40 N.

learn.reallife: Ball bearings in the wheels of Indian Railways' bogies replace sliding with rolling, saving huge amounts of energy.

games.title: Static or kinetic friction?
items: Box at rest, pushed gently
Feet on the ground while walking
Book sliding across a desk
Car tyres skidding with locked brakes
Block resting on a slope
Sledge gliding down a snowy hill

games.title: Laws of friction
items: Limiting friction depends on the area of contact.
It is independent of area.
μ_k is usually less than μ_s.
It is easier to keep a body sliding than to start it.
Static friction always equals μ_s N.
That is only its maximum; it adjusts up to that limit.
Rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction.
Hence wheels.
If tan θ of an incline exceeds μ_s, a block on it starts to slide.
θ exceeds the angle of repose.

quiz.q: A 20 kg crate is on a floor with μ_s = 0.4 (g = 10 m s⁻²). The minimum horizontal force needed to just start it moving, in N, is
quiz.mistake: Uses the weight instead of μN

quiz.q: The same crate (20 kg) is pushed with 50 N and does not move. The friction force on it in N is
quiz.explain: Static friction self-adjusts to match the 50 N push.
quiz.mistake: Assumes friction is always at its maximum

quiz.q: A block just begins to slide on an incline at 30°. The coefficient of static friction is (tan 30° = 0.577)
quiz.explain: At the angle of repose, μ_s = tan θ = 0.577.
quiz.mistake: Uses sin 30° or cos 30°

quiz.q: A 5 kg block slides on a floor with μ_k = 0.2 (g = 10 m s⁻²). The kinetic friction in N is
quiz.mistake: Uses μ_k × m without g

quiz.q: Limiting friction between two surfaces is
options: Proportional to the normal reaction and independent of area of contact
Proportional to the area of contact
quiz.explain: These are the empirical laws of friction.
quiz.mistake: Thinks bigger contact area means more friction

quiz.q: Why is it easier to keep a box sliding than to start it moving?
options: Normal force decreases when it moves
quiz.explain: Kinetic friction is smaller than limiting static friction.
quiz.mistake: Thinks friction vanishes in motion

quiz.q: A box slides with kinetic friction 40 N. Its speed doubles. The kinetic friction becomes approximately (in N)
quiz.explain: Kinetic friction is roughly independent of speed.
quiz.mistake: Thinks friction grows with speed

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Ball bearings reduce friction in machines.
Reason (R): Ball bearings are usually made of hardened steel.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, but the material is not the reason; bearings work because rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction.
quiz.mistake: Picks a true but irrelevant fact

teach.ask: Gappu pushes a pebble softly and it doesn't move, then pushes harder and it slides. He thinks friction 'switched on'. Explain static, kinetic and rolling friction.
teach.praise: Static friction matches my push up to μN, then kinetic friction (smaller) takes over. Rolling is easiest of all!
teach.nudge: Was friction there before the pebble moved? What is the most it can be? What changes after sliding starts?

topics.title: Friction at work: walking, trucks, connected blocks and lifts

learn.hook: Without friction you couldn't walk, a car couldn't move, and a lift ride would feel very strange. Let's put forces to work.
points: Friction is essential: static friction from the road drives a car forward and lets us walk. Lubricants and ball bearings reduce unwanted friction in machines.
A box on a truck floor (μ_s) stays put as long as the truck's acceleration a ≤ μ_s g, because static friction is the only horizontal force on the box.
Block m₁ on a table (μ_k) tied over a pulley to a hanging m₂: a = (m₂ − μ_k m₁)g/(m₁ + m₂) and T = m₂(g − a).
Atwood machine (m₁ > m₂): a = (m₁ − m₂)g/(m₁ + m₂), T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂).
Lift: apparent weight N = m(g + a) when accelerating up, m(g − a) when accelerating down, 0 in free fall, and mg at constant velocity.

example.q: A 2 kg block on a table (μ_k = 0.1) is tied by a string over a pulley to a hanging 3 kg block (g = 10 m s⁻²). Find a and T.
steps: a = (m₂g − μ_k m₁g)/(m₁ + m₂) = (30 − 2)/5 = 5.6 m s⁻².
Hanging block: m₂g − T = m₂a → T = 3(10 − 5.6) = 13.2 N.
Check table block: T − 2 = 2 × 5.6 → T = 13.2 N ✓.

learn.reallife: Riding a lift at a Mumbai high-rise, you feel heavier as it starts upward and lighter as it starts downward: the normal force from the floor changes.

games.title: Lift motion ↔ apparent weight of 60 kg person (g = 10 m s⁻²)

items.q: Box on truck, μs = 0.3: max a (m/s²)
50 kg in lift accelerating up at 1 m/s²: N (N)
50 kg in lift accelerating down at 1 m/s²: N (N)

quiz.q: A box lies on a truck floor with μ_s = 0.2 (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). The maximum acceleration of the truck for the box not to slip, in m s⁻², is
quiz.explain: Static friction μ_s mg is the only horizontal force: a_max = μ_s g = 0.2 × 9.8 = 1.96 m s⁻².
quiz.mistake: Forgets g or divides by μ

quiz.q: Masses 5 kg and 3 kg hang over a frictionless pulley (Atwood machine, g = 10 m s⁻²). The acceleration in m s⁻² is
quiz.mistake: Divides by the difference instead of the sum

quiz.q: For the same Atwood machine (5 kg and 3 kg, g = 10 m s⁻²), the tension in N is
quiz.mistake: Takes T equal to one weight

quiz.q: A 70 kg man stands in a lift accelerating upward at 2 m s⁻² (g = 10 m s⁻²). The floor pushes him with (in N)
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the acceleration

quiz.q: The same man in a lift moving down at constant speed has an apparent weight (in N) of
quiz.explain: Constant velocity means a = 0, so N = mg = 700 N.
quiz.mistake: Thinks downward motion reduces the reading

quiz.q: A 4 kg block on a frictionless table is tied over a pulley to a hanging 1 kg block (g = 10 m s⁻²). The acceleration in m s⁻² is
quiz.explain: a = m₂g/(m₁ + m₂) = 10/5 = 2 m s⁻².
quiz.mistake: Uses only the hanging mass

quiz.q: What force actually makes a car accelerate forward on a road?
options: The engine pushing the car directly
Static friction from the road on the tyres
quiz.explain: The tyres push the road backward; the road's static friction pushes the car forward.
quiz.mistake: Thinks internal engine forces alone accelerate the car

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A person in a freely falling lift feels weightless.
Reason (R): In free fall, gravity stops acting on the person.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true because the floor's normal force becomes zero. R is false: gravity still acts; that is why the person falls.
quiz.mistake: Thinks weightlessness means no gravity

teach.ask: Gappu is riding in a lift and feels heavy at the start and light near the top. Explain using N = m(g ± a), and why friction is needed to walk.
teach.praise: The floor pushes harder when the lift speeds up upward, and less when it speeds up downward. And friction lets me walk!
teach.nudge: What does the floor's push equal when the lift accelerates upward? Downward?

topics.title: Circular motion: centripetal force and level roads

learn.hook: A motorbike rider taking a sharp turn on a wet road skids out. The road's friction simply could not supply enough centripetal force.
points: Circular motion needs a net force towards the centre: f_c = mv²/R (the centripetal force).
Centripetal force is not a new kind of force. It is supplied by existing forces: tension (stone on string), gravity (planets), friction (car on road), normal force (wall of death).
Car on a level road: static friction provides mv²/R, so mv²/R ≤ μ_s mg → v_max = √(μ_s R g), independent of mass.
Cyclist or car on a level turn: if v² > μ_s R g, it skids outward. Slow down or reduce sharpness (increase R).

example.q: A car takes a level turn of radius 20 m with μ_s = 0.5 (g = 10 m s⁻²). What is the maximum safe speed?
steps: v_max = √(μ_s R g).
= 10 m s⁻¹ = 36 km h⁻¹.

learn.reallife: Road signs on ghat roads of the Western Ghats warn of sharp curves because the friction available limits safe turning speed.

items.q: m = 2 kg, v = 4 m/s, R = 2 m: Fc (N)

quiz.q: A 0.5 kg stone is whirled in a horizontal circle of radius 1 m at 4 m s⁻¹. The tension (centripetal force) in N is
quiz.mistake: Forgets to square v

quiz.q: A cyclist goes round a level curve of radius 3 m at 5 m s⁻¹ with μ_s = 0.1 (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). Will he slip?
options: Yes, because v² = 25 exceeds μ_s R g = 2.94
No, because v² is less than μ_s R g
quiz.explain: Safe only if v² ≤ μ_s R g; 25 > 2.94, so friction cannot supply mv²/R.
quiz.mistake: Thinks static friction is unlimited

quiz.q: The maximum safe speed on a level curve does not depend on
quiz.explain: v_max = √(μ_s R g); mass cancels.
quiz.mistake: Thinks heavier vehicles can go faster

quiz.q: For a car on a level road with μ_s = 0.6 and R = 60 m (g = 10 m s⁻²), v_max in m s⁻¹ is
quiz.mistake: Forgets the square root

quiz.q: Centripetal force is best described as
options: The net force towards the centre, provided by real forces such as tension or friction
A new force that appears in circular motion
quiz.explain: It is a role played by existing forces, not a separate force.
quiz.mistake: Thinks centripetal force is an extra force to add

quiz.q: A car of mass 1000 kg moves on a level circular road of radius 50 m at 10 m s⁻¹. The friction force needed in N is
quiz.mistake: Divides by v instead of squaring it

quiz.q: If the speed of a car on a curve is doubled, the friction force needed to keep it on the same curve becomes how many times the original?
quiz.explain: f = mv²/R ∝ v².
quiz.mistake: Thinks f ∝ v

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A car can take a level curve at any speed if its tyres are new.
Reason (R): The static friction available cannot exceed μ_s mg.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: v_max = √(μ_s R g) limits the speed whatever the tyres. R is true.
quiz.mistake: Thinks friction is unlimited

teach.ask: Gappu thinks 'centripetal force' is a mystery force that appears whenever things go round. Explain what really supplies it on a level road, and the speed limit.
teach.praise: Centripetal force is a job, not a new force! On a flat road, friction does the job, up to √(μRg).
teach.nudge: Which real force pulls the car towards the centre on a level road? Is there a speed limit?

topics.title: Banked roads: optimum and maximum safe speed

learn.hook: Ever noticed that the outer edge of a highway curve is raised? That tilt lets the road itself help steer the car.
points: On a road banked at θ, the normal force N tilts inward. Equations (friction f down the slope): N cos θ = mg + f sin θ and N sin θ + f cos θ = mv²/R.
With f ≤ μ_s N, the maximum safe speed is v_max = √[Rg(μ_s + tan θ)/(1 − μ_s tan θ)].
Optimum speed (no friction needed): v₀ = √(Rg tan θ). At this speed, wear on tyres is least.
Banking raises v_max above the level-road value √(μ_s R g), which is why race tracks and highway curves are banked.

example.q: A curve of radius 90 m is banked with tan θ = 1/3, and μ_s = 0.5 (g = 10 m s⁻²). Find the optimum and maximum safe speeds.
example.answer: v₀ ≈ 17.3 m s⁻¹, v_max = 30 m s⁻¹

learn.reallife: Cycle velodromes have steeply banked tracks, and highway curves are gently banked, so that vehicles can corner faster and more safely than on flat ground.

games.title: Deriving the optimum banking speed
items: Draw N perpendicular to the banked road and mg downward
Set friction to zero
Vertical: N cos θ = mg
Horizontal: N sin θ = mv²/R
Divide: tan θ = v²/(Rg), so v₀ = √(Rg tan θ)

games.title: Banking facts
items: On a banked road, part of the normal force provides the centripetal force.
N sin θ points to the centre.
At the optimum speed, friction is needed to keep the car on the road.
At v₀ no friction is needed.
Banking lets a car take a curve faster than on a level road with the same μ_s.
v_max increases.
The optimum speed depends on the mass of the car.
v₀ = √(Rg tan θ) has no mass.
If μ_s = 0, a car can still take a banked curve safely at v₀.
N alone provides the needed force.

quiz.q: A road of radius 40 m is banked at 45° (g = 10 m s⁻²). The optimum speed in m s⁻¹ is
quiz.mistake: Forgets the square root

quiz.q: At the optimum speed on a banked road, the centripetal force is provided by
options: The vertical component of the normal force
The horizontal component of the normal force
quiz.explain: With no friction, N sin θ = mv²/R.
quiz.mistake: Thinks friction is always needed

quiz.q: A track of radius 100 m is banked with tan θ = 0.1 (g = 10 m s⁻²). The optimum speed in m s⁻¹ is
quiz.mistake: Forgets tan θ

quiz.q: On a banked road with friction, which expression gives v_max?
quiz.explain: Friction acts down the slope at v_max, giving the plus sign in the numerator.

quiz.q: Radius 90 m, tan θ = 0.25, μ_s = 0.6 (g = 10 m s⁻²). Note (0.6 + 0.25)/(1 − 0.15) = 1. The maximum safe speed in m s⁻¹ is

quiz.q: For the same road (R = 90 m, tan θ = 0.25, g = 10 m s⁻²), the optimum speed in m s⁻¹ is

quiz.q: Why are railway tracks on curves built with the outer rail higher than the inner rail?
options: So that a component of the normal force supplies the centripetal force, reducing wear and the risk of derailing
To increase friction between wheels and rails
quiz.explain: Banking (cant) makes N sin θ help provide mv²/R, so the rails' sideways push on the wheel flanges is reduced.
quiz.mistake: Thinks banking is mainly for drainage

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The optimum speed on a banked road is independent of the mass of the vehicle.
Reason (R): v₀ = √(Rg tan θ) contains no mass term.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Mass cancels when dividing N sin θ = mv²/R by N cos θ = mg. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks heavier cars need different banking

teach.ask: Gappu asks why highway curves are tilted, and what speed a car should go so it doesn't even need friction. Explain banking.
teach.praise: The tilt makes the normal force lean in and do the turning. At √(Rg tan θ), no friction needed at all!
teach.nudge: Which force leans inward on a banked road? What is the speed at which friction is not needed?

topics.title: Solving mechanics problems with free-body diagrams

learn.hook: Most mistakes in mechanics come from one thing: forgetting a force or adding one that isn't there. Free-body diagrams fix that.
points: Step 1: draw a schematic diagram showing all bodies, supports and connections (strings, pulleys, springs).
Step 2: choose a convenient part as your system and draw its free-body diagram (FBD) showing only that body.
Step 3: show all EXTERNAL forces on it (weight, normal, tension, friction, applied), known and unknown, with directions. Do not include forces the body exerts on others.
Step 4: apply F = ma to the chosen system. When switching to another body, use the third law for the force between them.
Example: block B (3 kg) resting on block A (5 kg) on the floor (g = 10 m s⁻²): B pushes A down with 30 N; the floor pushes A up with 80 N.

example.q: A 3 kg block B rests on a 5 kg block A, which rests on the floor (g = 10 m s⁻²). Find the forces on A.
steps: FBD of B: weight 30 N down, normal from A 30 N up.
Third law: B pushes A down with 30 N.
FBD of A: weight 50 N down, 30 N down from B, floor's normal N up.
Equilibrium: N = 50 + 30 = 80 N.
example.answer: 30 N down from B, 50 N weight, 80 N up from floor

learn.reallife: IIT JEE toppers swear by one habit: draw the FBD before writing any equation. It works just as well for your CBSE paper.

games.title: The four-step method
items: Draw a schematic diagram of the set-up
Choose a body or part as the system
Draw its free-body diagram with all external forces
Apply Newton's second law to that system
Use the third law to move to the next body

games.title: Include in the FBD of a book resting on a table?
items: Weight of the book (Earth's pull)
Normal force of the table on the book
Force of the book on the table
Weight of the table
Book's pull on the Earth

quiz.q: In a free-body diagram of a body, we show
options: Forces the body exerts on others
Both action and reaction of each pair
All external forces acting on that body
quiz.explain: An FBD isolates one body and shows only the forces acting ON it.
quiz.mistake: Includes forces exerted BY the body

quiz.q: A 2 kg block rests on top of a 6 kg block on the floor (g = 10 m s⁻²). The normal force from the floor on the lower block in N is
quiz.explain: Floor supports both: (2 + 6) × 10 = 80 N.
quiz.mistake: Counts only the lower block's weight

quiz.q: A 2 kg block rests on top of a 6 kg block on the floor (g = 10 m s⁻²). The upward force (in N) exerted by the lower block on the upper block is
quiz.explain: The upper block is in equilibrium: normal from below = its weight = 20 N upward.
quiz.mistake: Includes the lower block's weight

quiz.q: Two blocks of 4 kg and 6 kg in contact on a frictionless floor are pushed by 20 N applied to the 4 kg block. The acceleration in m s⁻² is
quiz.explain: Treat both as one system: a = 20/10 = 2 m s⁻².
quiz.mistake: Uses only one block's mass

quiz.q: In the same set-up (20 N on 4 kg block pushing a 6 kg block), the contact force between the blocks in N is
quiz.explain: FBD of the 6 kg block: F_contact = 6 × 2 = 12 N.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the full 20 N is transmitted

quiz.q: When applying the second law to the whole stack of two blocks, the forces between the blocks
quiz.explain: They are an action–reaction pair inside the system and cancel.
quiz.mistake: Treats internal forces as external

quiz.q: A horse pulls a cart forward. Which force makes the horse–cart system accelerate?
options: The ground's friction on the horse's hooves (minus friction on the cart)
quiz.explain: Horse–cart forces are internal. The ground's forces are external.
quiz.mistake: Picks an internal force as the cause

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): To find the tension in a rope joining two blocks, we draw the free-body diagram of one block.
Reason (R): Tension is internal to the two-block system and does not appear when the system is treated as a whole.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Isolating one block makes the tension external to it, so it appears in that FBD. R explains why we must isolate.
quiz.mistake: Thinks tension can be found from the whole system

teach.ask: Gappu wants to find the push between two boxes being shoved across the floor, but keeps adding the wrong forces. Teach him the four-step free-body method.
teach.praise: Isolate one box, draw only forces ON it, apply F = ma, then use the third law for the next box. So tidy!
teach.nudge: Which forces go in the diagram of one box? How do you move from one box to the other?
